overview: The Great Seljuk Empire, founded when Tughril took Nishapur in 1037, brought Oghuz Turkic rule to Iran, Iraq and Anatolia under a Persian administration. Its sultans protected the Abbasid caliphs, built madrasas and mosques, and opened Anatolia to the Turks.

items.text: The vizier Nizam al-Mulk and his rival Taj al-Mulk added the two great brick domes to the Friday Mosque of Isfahan in 1086 and 1088.
Persian poetry, calligraphy and lustre ceramics flourished under Seljuk patronage; Omar Khayyam wrote the quatrains later gathered as the Rubaiyat.
Nizam al-Mulk founded the Nizamiyya of Baghdad, first of a network of madrasas teaching Shafi'i law and theology.
Alp Arslan's victory over the Byzantines at Manzikert opened Anatolia to Turkic settlement.
Nizam al-Mulk's Book of Government set out the Persian art of kingship for the sultans.
The Jalali calendar, computed by Omar Khayyam and colleagues for Malik Shah, fixed the year to the spring equinox with an error of about one day in 3,770 years, less than the Gregorian calendar's.
Khayyam's treatise on algebra classified cubic equations and solved them with conic sections.
The Turkic settlement of Anatolia that followed Manzikert led to the Sultanate of Rum and, in time, the Ottomans.
The madrasa became the standard school of Sunni learning.

fall.text: After Malik Shah's death in 1092 the empire split among his heirs and their atabegs. The last sultan of Iraq, Tughril III, was killed in 1194 by the Khwarazmshah Tekish, who took Iran; the Seljuks of Rum in Anatolia lasted until 1308.
